idiom_name: abstract `clone()` on the base type with a covariant `@Override` (deliberately not `Cloneable`/`Object.clone`)
implementation_notes: Java supplies a cloning mechanism, but it is the one nobody should use: `Cloneable` contains no `clone` method, `Object.clone()` is protected and requires the `super.clone()` chain, it bypasses constructors, and it throws a checked `CloneNotSupportedException` while specifying only a shallow copy - Bloch's Effective Java devotes an item to overriding it 'judiciously' and recommends copy constructors or static factories instead. The dependable realization of the pattern is the plain hand-written one: `public abstract Shape clone()` on the base type, overridden in every concrete class with a covariant return (`public Circle clone() { return new Circle(radius); }`, allowed since Java 5) and a copy constructor as its body. For a closed hierarchy, Java 21's sealed interfaces plus record patterns and exhaustive pattern `switch` (JEP 440/441) copy through the base type with compiler-checked coverage and no clone method at all.
pitfalls: `Cloneable`/`Object.clone()` are the classic trap: no clone method on the interface, protected visibility, an unenforceable `super.clone()` convention, final fields and package-visible state that `super.clone()` must fix, plus a checked exception - do not extend `Cloneable` in new code.

A hand-written clone body is shallow unless you make it deep: `new Circle(radius)` above is correct only because the field is a primitive; every mutable field (arrays, collections, nested objects) must be copied explicitly or the clone aliases the original.

Covariance only helps callers whose static type is the subclass; a caller holding `Shape` gets `Shape` back and must cast, and a forgotten override in a concrete class is a compile error only while the base method stays abstract (a non-abstract default silently returns the wrong type).
sources: Bloch, Effective Java (3rd ed.), Item 13 'Override clone judiciously' - prefer copy constructors or static factories.

variants.name: Sealed hierarchy + exhaustive switch copy (Java 21)
variants.idiom_name: exhaustive `switch` over a sealed interface with record patterns
variants.implementation_notes: For a closed hierarchy, Java 21 record patterns plus pattern matching for `switch` (JEP 440/441) express the copy as a checked dispatch table instead of a virtual method: a `switch` over the sealed interface whose cases destructure the records (`case Circle(double r) -> new Circle(r)`) is exhaustive without a `default`, and the compiler rejects the code when a new permitted subtype appears. Prefer it when the subtype set is intentionally closed and the copies are structural (immutable records); it cannot serve an open hierarchy (third-party subtypes) and inverts dispatch from the object to the caller.
pitfalls: Every exhaustive switch over the sealed hierarchy must be updated when a new permitted subtype is added - that is the safety feature, but the copy tables live in the callers, not in the classes.

A sealed hierarchy that changes after its switches were compiled can make an exhaustive switch fail at run time with `MatchException`, so keep the hierarchy and its switches in the same artifact/release.

Record patterns copy only the declared components: derived, cached or lazily computed state is not part of the pattern and must be reconstructed explicitly, and mutable components are still shared between original and copy.
